opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, this is something I go back and forth on a lot. I don't think I have a confident answer, and I'm a little suspicious of anyone who does.

I come at it from security, and in security the default instinct is that openness is good. You publish the attack, you release the code, because the defenders benefit more than the attackers. Attackers usually have the capability anyway, and sunlight is how things get fixed. For most of my career I've believed that pretty strongly, and for most of the models we've had so far I think it's been right. Releasing weights has let people like me actually study these systems. We find the failure modes and the privacy leaks, and we understand what's going on instead of taking a company's word for it.

But that argument rests on assumptions. It assumes the harm from misuse is bounded, that defenders can patch things, and that the capability is going to diffuse anyway. With a buffer overflow, all of that holds. With a model that meaningfully helps someone do something catastrophic and irreversible, I'm not sure it does. You can't patch the world after the fact. Once weights are out, they're out forever. That asymmetry, where release is irreversible and holding back is reversible, matters a lot to me when I'm uncertain.

So where I end up is less "open is good" or "closed is good" and more "what is the actual marginal capability this specific model adds, and how would we know?" The honest problem is we're often bad at measuring that. Our evaluations underestimate what models can do, because people find better ways to elicit capabilities after release. If you're uncertain and your measurements are biased low, that should push you toward some caution at the frontier.

At the same time, I worry about the opposite failure: "safety" becoming a convenient excuse to concentrate power in a handful of labs and lock out independent researchers. That's a real cost too. So I'd like to see things like structured access for researchers, so you don't face a binary choice between fully open and fully closed.

The short version: I think for most models that exist today, broad distribution has been net positive. I don't think that automatically extends to every future model, and the thing I'd most want is better ways of telling the difference before we find out the hard way.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the honest answer is that I'm genuinely uncertain, and I try not to pretend otherwise. My background is in finding ways to break things, so my instinct is to assume that any capability you ship will eventually be misused by someone. That's not a controversial prediction; it's just the base rate.

But the question isn't whether open models will be misused. Of course they will. The question is what the counterfactual looks like. If you don't release something, does the harm actually go away, or does it just get delayed by six months until someone else trains the same thing? And in the meantime, who got to study the model, red-team it, build defenses against it, understand its failure modes? Historically in security, the people who argued for keeping things secret were often wrong. Secrecy around vulnerabilities mostly protected vendors, not users.

So I have a lot of sympathy for the open-release position, and I think the track record so far mostly supports it. The models that have been released openly haven't caused the kind of catastrophe people worried about. The attacks we've demonstrated, like extracting training data or jailbreaking safety filters, are real, but they're the sort of thing you want discovered in public by researchers rather than discovered quietly by someone with bad intentions.

Where I get nervous is that "the track record so far is fine" is exactly the argument that stops working at the point where it matters. Every capability jump that was safe to release is evidence that the next one is also safe, right up until it isn't. And once the weights are out, there's no recall. You can't patch a model that's sitting on ten thousand hard drives. That asymmetry, where the decision is irreversible but the evidence for it is always backward-looking, is the thing I don't know how to resolve.

So what I actually try to do is be concrete rather than philosophical. Instead of asking "should models be open," I ask "what specifically could this model do that the previous one couldn't, and does that change the threat model in a way I can articulate?" Most of the time, when I do that exercise honestly, the answer is that the marginal uplift is small and the benefits to the research community are large. But I want to keep doing the exercise each time rather than settling into a position, because the day the answer changes, I'd like to notice.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s real uncertainty here, and I don’t think we should pretend that we already know the right answer. There are substantial benefits to making models widely available: more people can study them, understand their failures, and build useful things with them. But as models become more capable, we have to take seriously the possibility that distributing them also makes harmful activities easier.

The question I’d want to ask is: how much does this particular model change what someone can actually do? Does it give them information they could easily find elsewhere, or does it let them carry out something they otherwise couldn’t? Those are different situations, and measuring that difference is hard.

There’s also an asymmetry in the decision. You can decide to release a model later, but once you’ve released the weights, you can’t really take them back. That’s a reason for caution as capabilities increase. It isn’t, by itself, an argument that everything should be closed forever. I’d want us to keep testing our assumptions and be willing to change the release strategy when the evidence changes.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s real uncertainty here, and I don’t think we should pretend we know exactly where the right boundary is. There are substantial benefits to making models widely available. People can study them, understand their failures, and build things that a small number of companies wouldn’t think to build. As a researcher, having access to the actual model lets you answer questions that you just can’t answer through an API.

But releasing the weights is also a decision that’s very difficult to reverse. If a model turns out to enable some substantially harmful capability, you can’t recall all the copies. So I wouldn’t take the fact that openness has been beneficial so far as proof that every future model should be released.

For me, the question is: what changes because this particular model is available? Does it make some harmful task meaningfully easier than it already was? And how good is our evidence? I’d like us to get much better at measuring that, while recognizing that our evaluations will have blind spots. You can favor broad access and still think that, as capabilities increase, some releases deserve more caution.
